A REPEATED QUESTION

Where does the real axis come from?

Each luminous curve is a numerical preimage of the real axis. Nearby points are sent to opposite half-planes. Follow a point to see the geometry become dynamics.

Compare orders to identify structures that stabilize. Higher orders cost more and amplify rounding.

Compute six frames once, then play them smoothly.

Crossfades blend rendered images, not fractional mathematical orders. The orbit follows the lower integer order during a blend. Pan, zoom, or change mode to leave playback and recompute.

THE CONSTRUCTION

Fold twice. Shrink once.

Start with P(z) = 1 − az² at a ≈ 1.40115518909205. Let sₙ = P²ⁿ(0). The normalized return maps fₙ(z) = P²ⁿ(sₙz) / sₙ approach the quadratic Feigenbaum fixed point near the critical point.

f(z) = −f(f(λz)) / λ
λ ≈ 0.3995352805 · α = −1/λ ≈ −2.502907875
READ THE MOTION

A complicated fold becomes a contraction.

In the limit, f(h(z)) = −λf(z), with h(z) = f(λz). The small image-plane view shows this relationship: the transformed orbit alternates direction and contracts toward zero. In the z plane it approaches the first positive zero x₀ of f.

Skeleton → Figure 5. Nested scales → Figures 6–7. The orbit inset illustrates the linearizing equation in §2.2.

NUMERICAL HONESTY

A window into the limit.

This is a double-precision, finite-order experiment, not a reconstruction of the entire maximal analytic extension. Near the critical point the return maps approximate f; far away, structures may be artifacts of the finite polynomial. Compare orders before interpreting a feature.

Dark pixels exceed the evaluation cutoff; they do not prove a point is outside the paper’s dense domain. Colored regions show the sign or argument of fₙ, not basin membership. Thin curves are sampled boundaries, so deep zoom requires recomputation.
